The Yellowstripe barracuda (Sphyraena chrysotaenia) is a commercially important scombrid predator inhabiting the eastern Mediterranean and Red Sea. Field surveys indicate that larval emergence from the pelagic egg occurs after a brief incubation period, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae carrying a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0016 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0016 grams]. This minimal initial mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy typical of sphyraenid larvae, where endogenous yolk reserves sustain development during the non-feeding prolarval stage. Following yolk-sac resorption, the first exogenous feeding onset coincides with mouth opening and retinal differentiation, marking a critical trophic switch that determines early survival. The pelagic larval phase is characterized by rapid fin ray ossification and a pronounced allometric shift as individuals progress through preflexion and postflexion stages. Under typical thermal conditions measured in coastal nursery habitats at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the maximum reproductive rate has been inferred from ovarian analyses; females release approximately 274 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 274 eggs per spawning event], with multiple spawning events occurring throughout the season [F_R_i = multiple spawning events occurring throughout the season] and a remarkably high daily fecundity that underscores the species' capacity for rapid population turnover.

Sexual maturation in female Yellowstripe barracuda involves a progressive period of gonad development culminating in the first spawning event. Studies of captive-reared individuals and wild-caught specimens from the Gulf of Suez indicate that females attain puberty at a fork length of 19.3 centimeters [Lp = 19.3 centimeters], a relatively modest body size compared to other barracuda species. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 36.4 grams [Wwp = 36.4 grams], derived from length-weight regressions that demonstrate isometric growth patterns within this population. This size at maturity allows females to begin participating in spawning aggregations during their second year of life, contributing to the species' early onset of reproductive activity. Histological examination of ovarian tissue reveals that vitellogenesis onset is synchronized with seasonal temperature cues, and gravid individuals are typically encountered from April through September. The age at puberty corresponds approximately to 18 months after hatching, a duration that reflects the rapid growth rates sustained in the warm, productive waters this species occupies.

The maximum recorded body size for Yellowstripe barracuda in the eastern Mediterranean suggests an ultimate fork length of 32.2 centimeters [Li = 32.2 centimeters], a value consistent across multiple independent population surveys conducted over the past two decades. The corresponding ultimate wet weight derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship is 161.5 grams [Wwi = 161.5 grams], indicating a relatively slender, fusiform body plan adapted for high-speed pursuit of small pelagic prey. This asymptotic body size is attained after approximately three to four years of growth, during which juveniles undergo a habitat transition from shallow vegetated nurseries to open-water schooling aggregations. The growth trajectory exhibits a deceleration as individuals approach their maximum length, a pattern typical of determinate-growing teleosts where somatic investment gradually shifts toward reproductive effort. Comparative analyses within the genus Sphyraena indicate that S. chrysotaenia occupies an intermediate position in terms of adult body size, being notably smaller than the great barracuda but larger than several Indo-Pacific congeners of similar ecological niche.

Longevity data derived from otolith increment analysis indicate that the life span of Yellowstripe barracuda reaches 8 years [am = 8 years] under natural conditions, with the oldest confirmed individuals collected from relatively undisturbed populations in the Red Sea at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This value was recorded from specimens captured at a mean annual water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], a relatively warm regime that likely accelerates metabolic processes and reduces maximum potential lifespan compared to conspecifics in cooler peripheral habitats. The species exhibits rapid early growth, with young-of-the-year individuals reaching fork lengths of 12 to 15 centimeters by the end of their first growing season. Mortality rates are highest during the pelagic larval phase and early juvenile period, when predation pressure from planktivorous fishes and gelatinous zooplankton is intense. Survivorship stabilizes markedly after juvenile recruitment to benthic habitats, with adult annual mortality rates estimated at approximately 30 percent across most studied populations.

The reproductive ecology of this species is tightly coupled to temperature, with spawning activity intensifying when water temperatures exceed 25 °C and peaking at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the same thermal regime that maximizes larval developmental rates. Egg diameter measurements of 1.45 millimeters, which underpin the wet weight at birth calculation, are consistent with a pelagic reproductive strategy where buoyant, transparent eggs drift with ocean currents until hatching. The combination of elevated clutch sizes and extended spawning seasons results in an extraordinarily high lifetime reproductive potential for a fish of this body size, placing S. chrysotaenia among the more fecund members of the genus Sphyraena. Understanding these reproductive parameters is essential for developing effective fisheries management strategies in the face of increasing exploitation pressure across the species' range.
